verification_vocabulary: Same as GRAPH-FORMAT.md: bibliographic_metadata_checked = identity/edition checked against the record named; supporting_page_checked = an abstract, publisher summary, contents page, review text or opening text was read for the specific point in the note; unverified = could not be confirmed, kept out of proposed sources. No book was read in full. Subtitles follow Crossref, Open Library or the citation graph's bibliographic strings; places of publication follow publisher convention and were not separately checked.

records.citation: Ian McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History,” Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (December 2000): 617–45, doi:10.3138/chr.81.4.616.

verification.checked_against: Crossref DOI record (CHR 81:4, December 2000; Crossref gives 616–678 for the forum span); OpenAlex abstract (English and French); page range 616–645 as cited by Parnaby (2019); Crossref journal listing for CHR 81:4 (https://api.crossref.org/journals/0008-3755/works?filter=from-pub-date:2000-12-01,until-pub-date:2000-12-31); Project MUSE record https://muse.jhu.edu/article/590654 (blocked; page range reported by search summary)
verification.note: Abstract read: the way past the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse" is a re/connaissance mapping the Canadian state as "a project of liberal rule in northern North America", through which "liberal order became the national-political ‘commonsense’". Article body unread; McKay’s phrases on liberty, equality and property and on keeping liberalism and capitalism analytically separate (p. 629) are known here only through Fecteau (2009). Page range revised 2026-10-12 (answers Q20): cite 617–45. The DOI begins at 616 (the abstract page); Project MUSE reportedly gives 616–645; Crossref and OpenAlex give 616–678, a metadata error (their CHR 81:4 ranges overlap). End page not yet checked against a PDF. The abstract does not define liberalism by liberty, equality and property: that trio is Fecteau's paraphrase, not a checked McKay quotation. The best checked opening formulation is McKay 2000, 620–1, as quoted by Fecteau ('a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism'). The 'cannot be conflated' line on capitalism is from McKay's 2009 reply (p. 385), not this essay.

records.reading: Canada as a project of liberal rule; liberal hegemony; a way past the social versus national-political impasse.

records.citation: Nancy Christie, “Revisiting Canada’s Project of Liberal Rule,” The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.

verification.checked_against: Carleton Underhill Review page read
verification.note: Text read: the framework gives coherence to a vast cultural and social literature; but McKay neglects republicanism, civic humanism and Ancien Régime sensibilities, over-emphasizes the state (Curtis: what McKay describes is "governmentality"), ignores religion as "a powerful vehicle in the creation of the liberal order", and his "definition of individualism based on property ownership" excludes women.

records.reading: Critique and proposed extension: religion, voluntary associations, the family, gender.

records.citation: Jean-Marie Fecteau, “Towards a Theory of Possible History? Ian McKay’s Idea of a ‘Liberal Order’,” The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.

verification.checked_against: Carleton Underhill Review page read
verification.note: Text read: quotes McKay (1994) on a "liberal capitalist order … based on possessive individualism"; McKay (2000, 629) that liberalism and capitalism must be kept "analytically separate"; McKay (2009, 385) that they "cannot be conflated" yet after the 1840s "could not be easily separated"; and McKay's trio "liberty, equality, property". Fecteau objects that the trio is not a stable, unitary set and that the liberal order is not a single enterprise.

records.reading: Capitalism and liberalism distinguished; the property–liberty–equality definition contested.

records.citation: Martin Pâquet, “A Seductive Interpretation: Probing Ian McKay’s Prospectus,” The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.

verification.checked_against: Carleton Underhill Review page read
verification.note: Text read: names two explicit influences on the prospectus, Gramsci and Fernande Roy's Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988), which presents liberalism as founded on the supremacy of the individual and inviolable individual rights "including that of private property"; links the framework to studies of state formation and liberal social regulation; McKay's liberalism reifies the abstract individual and separates those who count as individuals from those who do not.

records.reading: The prospectus's Gramscian and francophone sources; the abstract individual.

records.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, “Radical Reasoning” (review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.

verification.checked_against: Carleton Underhill Review page read

Quotes McKay (RRR, 84) on the left pushing liberal order "to its definitional limits".

records.reading: Marxist critique: the framework avoids naming capitalism.
